red.focus: Recognize why law must protect people while enabling government to act.
red.summary: A state needs power to maintain public order, but the person subject to its rules has rights and interests of their own. Learn to identify who may act, who is affected, and what legal justification is required.
checklist: I can name a protected personal interest and the official act affecting it
I can distinguish government's useful goals from its legal powers
I can explain why even unpopular persons deserve legal protection

sections.title: Two needs can be legitimate
sections.body_md: A city limits access to a dangerous bridge after an engineering warning. People need safe infrastructure, but a delivery worker also needs to earn a living. Saying that safety matters does not end the inquiry, and neither does saying that freedom matters. Identify exactly what officials have done, which interests are restricted, and what law empowers them. Public power is not the same as a private person's freedom to act. Because the state can enforce its orders, its reasons require particular scrutiny.

sections.title: Power comes with boundaries
sections.body_md: A council may close roads under a valid emergency regulation, yet lack authority to punish residents who respectfully criticize the closure. Legal power is a grant limited by its source, purpose, and any applicable rights. A policy can be sensible while an official lacks permission to impose it in the chosen way. Conversely, a valid restriction need not be pleasant for every individual. The first question is not which participant seems likable; it is what authority and protection the legal order recognizes.

sections.title: Ask how the affected person is heard
sections.body_md: Suppose the bridge stays closed for months after repairs are complete. The worker needs a fair way to challenge continued restrictions, obtain reasons, and seek a lawful remedy. Participation, notice, and review can make government answerable without disabling legitimate safety measures. Different jurisdictions set different legal standards. A strong beginner's answer names the person, the governmental goal, the source of power, the relevant right, and the next authorized step for checking whether the limit remains justified.

yellow.focus: Compare Mill's harm principle with public paternalism.
yellow.summary: John Stuart Mill defended strong limits on coercion for a person's own good, while other thinkers justify some protective restrictions. Distinguish harm to others from self-regarding risk without assuming the distinction always settles existing law.
checklist: I can state the basic harm principle with its limits
I can distinguish paternalistic from third-party protective measures
I can apply lawful proportionality or rights tests to a concrete rule

sections.title: The harm principle asks whom conduct threatens
sections.body_md: In On Liberty (1859), Mill famously argued for limiting coercion over competent adults when their conduct concerns only themselves, while recognizing protection against harm to others as a reason for intervention. This is a political and moral principle, not a statute automatically binding every court. A helmet rule for adults may be defended as prevention of self-harm, while rules against reckless driving address danger to other people. Both still require attention to the governing legal system and the factual justification.
sections.audio_script: In On Liberty (1859), Mill famously argued for limiting coercion over competent adults when their conduct concerns only themselves, while recognizing protection against harm to others as a reason for intervention. sections.title: Paternalism can help or dominate
sections.body_md: A protective rule may prevent devastating injury, but it may also deny people meaningful control over their own lives. Paternalism describes interference intended to benefit the person restricted. Defenders point to severe risks, constrained decision-making, and social costs; critics emphasize autonomy, dignity, and the state's tendency to misjudge individual welfare. The analysis must not assume that any use of the word 'safety' proves third-party harm. Identify whose interests are protected and what less restrictive alternatives might exist.

Defenders point to severe risks, constrained decision-making, and social costs; critics emphasize autonomy, dignity, and the state's tendency to misjudge individual welfare. The analysis must not assume that any use of the word 'safety' proves third-party harm. Identify whose interests are protected and what less restrictive alternatives might exist.

sections.title: Turn philosophy into legal method
sections.body_md: A law school's debate about Mill is distinct from advising a client about current constitutional rights. For a specific restriction, locate the enabling law, identify any affected rights, determine the governing standard of review, and examine evidence supporting its purpose and fit. A court may permit a measure that Mill would criticize, or reject one that a political philosopher defends. Good jurisprudence can explain both what the law is and whether it should change, without disguising moral preference as binding authority.

orange.focus: Evaluate the relationship among Hobbesian order, Locke's rights, and Raz's authority.
orange.summary: Government can prevent destructive private conflict, but that alone may not justify every command. Compare security-based accounts of political obligation with rights-oriented limits and the service conception of authority.
checklist: I can contrast order-based and rights-based justifications
I can explain Raz's normal-justification idea without conflating validity and obedience
I can assess whether a particular official decision improves subjects' ability to act on reasons

sections.title: Order explains why institutions matter
sections.body_md: Thomas Hobbes emphasized the dangers of insecurity when no common authority can settle disputes; a sovereign's power could enable peace. John Locke placed greater weight on government securing rights and on limits to political power. These thinkers offer contrasting normative explanations, not templates copied wholesale into modern constitutions. A master's student should ask what insecurity a rule prevents, which rights it burdens, and which institution is authorized to impose it. The demand for public order cannot by itself resolve the limits of government.
sections.audio_script: Thomas Hobbes emphasized the dangers of insecurity when no common authority can settle disputes; a sovereign's power could enable peace. These thinkers offer contrasting normative explanations, not templates copied wholesale into modern constitutions. A master's student should ask what insecurity a rule prevents, which rights it burdens, and which institution is authorized to impose it. The demand for public order cannot by itself resolve the limits of government.

sections.title: Authority can serve, not merely command
sections.body_md: Joseph Raz's service conception asks when authority helps subjects better conform to reasons that already apply to them. In the normal-justification thesis, obeying an authority can sometimes improve conformity to those underlying reasons compared with acting alone. This is not a claim that every legally valid order is morally justified, nor that subjects lack any independent reasons to resist. It invites scrutiny of expertise, coordination, and whether the institution actually performs the function invoked to support its authority.

sections.title: Apply the test to a public agency
sections.body_md: An environmental agency adopts a technically grounded limit on emissions that cross property boundaries. The rule may coordinate action people cannot easily achieve individually. Yet the agency must still act within law, use reliable evidence, and respect rights and review. Its ability to help solve collective problems supports one argument for authority; its institutional failures may weaken that argument. Distinguish the legal question of statutory competence from the moral claim that obedience would better serve the reasons relevant to citizens.

black.focus: Construct a justified limit on state coercion within political pluralism.
black.summary: Liberty, coordinated welfare, and nondomination can collide when public decisions affect vulnerable groups. Defend a theory that distinguishes legal authority, its moral justification, and effective avenues of challenge.
checklist: I can differentiate legitimacy, legality, and moral duty
I can evaluate domination and exclusion in supposedly beneficial interventions
I can design public justification and oversight for coercive policy

sections.title: Legality does not settle legitimacy
sections.body_md: A legislature may validly pass a law that deeply burdens a minority community. Hart-style source-based validity may identify the rule as law without establishing a moral duty to obey it; rival theories may place justice more directly within legal interpretation. A doctoral response should state the theoretical disagreement rather than caricature positivism as blind obedience. Identify legal status, political justification, and individual obligation as separable propositions. Each demands an argument and may produce a different answer for the same statute.

Identify legal status, political justification, and individual obligation as separable propositions. Each demands an argument and may produce a different answer for the same statute.

sections.title: Power can be arbitrary without being violent
sections.body_md: A licensing regime might allow officials to deny applications for opaque reasons. Even if most applicants receive permits, those excluded may be dominated by discretionary power they cannot anticipate or contest. Republican theories of nondomination emphasize the problem of uncontrolled interference. Other approaches emphasize autonomy, participation, or distributive justice. A defensible comparison asks which harms each theory reveals and whether objective standards, reasons, and appeal actually reduce arbitrary dependence. Merely calling a rule neutral does not make its effects just.

sections.title: Design accountable coercion
sections.body_md: Propose clear legislative authorization, publicly available criteria, necessity or proportionality review where governing law requires, meaningful participation, and effective remedies for abuse. Explain why the scheme addresses a collective problem better than less restrictive alternatives. If expert decisions are needed, define how their evidence can be challenged without ignoring their competence. Separate reforms from presently binding requirements. A legitimate order should be explainable even to the person who loses: why the state acted, why this restriction was chosen, and how an error can be corrected.
